content:
By the time I met the Avatar, Cranefish Town had already learned how to build upward faster than it could learn how to live together.

The old colony streets had been widened twice in three years. Earth Kingdom stone houses leaned beside Fire Nation brick workshops, their roofs almost touching over alleys crowded with laundry, steam, and shouting vendors. New metal tracks cut through roads that had once been dirt. Every week another scaffold rose against the skyline. Every week another family arrived carrying its whole life in baskets, trunks, or whatever could be tied to the back of a cart.

I had come because towns like that always needed people who could count.

Not money exactly. People. Crates of medicine. Winter blankets. Work permits. Missing relatives. Which neighborhood had three wells and which had one broken pump. Which factory owner promised twelve-hour shifts and quietly demanded sixteen. I was a nonbender with neat handwriting, a stubborn dislike of lost paperwork, and the useful talent of remembering when someone had told me two different versions of the same story.

It was not glorious work.

It was work that mattered.

The morning Team Avatar arrived, I was standing knee-deep in a disagreement between a metalworker and a cabbage seller when the street bucked under my feet.

The first jolt knocked a stack of baskets sideways. The second cracked a wall.

Someone screamed, “Gas line!”

Then the world became motion.

I did not see Toph Beifong arrive. I felt the street change.

Stone lifted in a hard ridge beneath the collapsing wall and caught it before it crushed the people below. A girl—woman, really, though she was younger than I expected from the stories—stood barefoot in the dust with both hands spread, chin tilted toward the chaos as if the ground itself were giving her a report.

“Move!” she barked. “Unless somebody wants a building as a hat!”

People moved.

Water came next, sweeping along the gutter in a shining ribbon. Katara pulled it from three barrels and a burst pipe at once, coiling it around a line of fire that had licked out from beneath a workshop door. Her braid snapped over her shoulder as she turned. Nothing about her looked uncertain.

“Aang!” she shouted.

“I’ve got it!”

The answer came from above.

Aang dropped from the roof in a spiral of air, robes snapping around his legs. He landed lightly enough to make it look rude that the rest of us had to obey gravity. One palm turned. Wind punched smoke away from the street and up between the buildings.

For one absurd second, with ash blowing past his tattoos and his face set in concentration, he looked exactly like the statues.

Then he nearly stepped in a broken cabbage crate.

“Whoa—sorry!”

The cabbage seller stared at him.

Aang stared at the cabbage.

Toph snorted. “Great save, Twinkle Toes.”

The moment broke. I laughed before I could stop myself.

Toph’s head snapped in my direction.

“Oh, good,” she said. “Somebody appreciates me.”

“I appreciated the wall more.”

Her grin widened.

Katara reached us while Aang helped lift a fallen beam. “Are you hurt?” she asked me.

I looked down. Blood had soaked through the knee of my trousers where falling stone had caught me.

“Apparently.”

Her expression did something complicated: concern first, irritation second, the look of a healer who had already decided I was going to be difficult.

“Sit.”

“I’m working.”

“You’re bleeding.”

“So is the street.”

Toph laughed so loudly that two frightened children nearby looked at her instead of the smoke.

Katara folded her arms. “The street is not going to get infected.”

“I don’t know. Have you seen the canals?”

That earned the smallest twitch at the corner of her mouth.

“Sit.”

I sat.

Katara knelt beside me and pulled clean water from the skin at her hip. Blue light shimmered around her hands. The ache dulled almost immediately, though not enough to make me forget that I had spent the morning trying to convince workers not to store lamp oil next to furnace vents.

“Thank you,” I said, quieter.

“You’re welcome.” She glanced toward my satchel, where three ledgers had spilled onto the ground. “What were you doing here?”

“Trying to keep this district from killing itself with bad planning.”

“Any luck?”

“Ask me after lunch.”

Aang came over carrying one of my ledgers beneath his arm and a very offended cabbage under the other.

“I think this is yours.”

“The ledger or the cabbage?”

He looked at both as if the question had become unexpectedly philosophical. “The ledger.”

“Shame.”

His smile came quickly. That was the first thing about him that did not match the statues. Statues made him solemn. In person, joy lived close to the surface.

He handed me the book. “You keep the housing records?”

“Housing, food distribution, injury reports, wage disputes, missing permits, and occasionally cabbage casualties.”

“Sounds worse than fighting the Fire Lord,” Toph said.

Aang’s mouth tilted. “Some days.”

Katara finished binding my knee. “Aang.”

“I know.” His face changed. Not into the Avatar, exactly. Into someone carrying a weight that had learned how to settle onto his shoulders. “We were told there have been three industrial accidents this month.”

“Four,” I said.

All three looked at me.

“The fourth never made the official reports. A foreman paid the injured workers and told them they’d lose their jobs if they talked.”

Toph’s bare heel pressed into the street.

“Which factory?”

I pointed.

She turned toward the building without needing to follow my hand.

Katara’s expression sharpened. “You’re sure?”

“I wrote down the names myself.”

Aang crouched so we were closer to eye level. “Will they talk to us?”

“Maybe not to the Avatar.”

He winced, but he did not get defensive.

That surprised me more than the airbending.

“Who will they talk to?” he asked.

“Someone who knows what it costs to lose a week’s wages.”

Toph jerked her chin toward me. “Paperwork’s coming with us.”

“My name is not Paperwork.”

“Too late.”

Katara stood and offered me a hand. “Can you walk?”

I tested the knee. Tender, but steady.

“Yes.”

“Good,” she said. “Because if what you’re saying is true, we need someone who knows the workers.”

Aang looked pleased, almost relieved, as if being told what he did not know was a gift instead of an insult.

That, more than anything, made me say yes.

We spent the rest of the day going door to door.

The stories came slowly. A crushed hand. Burns hidden under sleeves. A woman whose husband had disappeared after refusing to work an unsafe furnace. Toph listened with her whole body, feet planted, jaw tightening whenever someone lied from fear. Katara asked careful questions and remembered every child’s name. Aang sat on doorsteps instead of looming over anyone. When an old man cursed the Avatar for caring more about harmony than rent, Aang let him finish.

“I can’t fix what I won’t listen to,” he said.

The old man stared at him for a long moment, then invited us inside.

By sunset, my satchel was twice as heavy with statements.

We climbed to the roof of the relief office to get out of the street. The city stretched around us in crooked layers of tile, brick, smoke, and scaffold.

Katara passed me a cup of tea.

Toph sat with both feet flat against the roof and announced that the building had terrible foundations.

“It has stood for forty years,” I said.

“Yeah. Out of spite.”

Aang laughed. He sat cross-legged beside me, shoulder almost touching mine.

“Do you always argue with people five minutes after meeting them?” he asked.

“Only important people.”

Toph slapped the roof in approval.

Katara hid a smile behind her cup.

Aang looked out over Cranefish Town. For a moment the playfulness left him. “This place could become something no one’s seen before. People from every nation living together. Not as guests. Not as occupiers. Just… people.”

“It could,” I said.

He glanced at me. “You don’t sound convinced.”

“I’m convinced by drains that work, wages people can live on, and walls that don’t fall on cabbage sellers.”

Toph barked a laugh.

Katara’s eyes warmed.

Aang considered me, then nodded. “Okay.”

“Okay?”

“Then help us build that version.”

The invitation landed harder than I expected.

I had spent years being useful in temporary places. Useful people were easy to welcome and easy to leave behind.

Toph tilted her head toward me. Her grin softened by a fraction.

My heartbeat must have betrayed something, because she said, “Uh-oh.”

“What?”

“Paperwork’s thinking feelings.”

“I hate you already.”

“No, you don’t.”

Katara laughed.

Aang’s smile turned toward me, bright as open sky.

And somewhere beneath us, through brick and beam and old stone, the city kept moving.

For the first time since I had arrived, I wondered what it might feel like to stop treating it as a place I was passing through.

The thought stayed with me.
